• Early exit polls show the election could be deadlocked and it may be weeks before a clear winner emerges.
• Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party is likely to be the largest in the Knesset, according to polling.
• It remains unclear whether he will be able to form a coalition government.
• Israelis have turned out in record numbers to vote in the election.

Highest voter turnout in more than two decades
Voter turnout was 77.7 per cent, Israel's Central Elections Committee said.
That makes it the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in the previous election in 2022.
Photos capture Israelis heading to the polls
Result will test unity of anti-Netanyahu camp

Netanyahu’s battle now is the narrative of the outcome of these elections. How will he turn his defeat into a victory? The numbers are clear. At the last election, his party got 32 mandates out of the 120 members in the Israeli parliament. In these elections, the leading exit polls are showing he will receive no more than 25.
Not only that, his coalition, which has a majority in the current parliament, will be getting 50 seats while his opponents will be receiving 70 seats.

Nevertheless, Netanyahu has been working on a new spin. He is predicted to get more seats than Eisenkot’s party. He knows that that fact plays no role, as all governments have to build a governing coalition. That was the case when Tzipi Livni’s party received more seats then Netanyahu back in February 2009, and that did not prevent him from forming the coalition and emerging as the winner as he had more partners to cooperate with.

In order to convince the public that he was not outright defeated, he will undermine the Arab votes. These elections, the Arab Palestinian minority in Israel went out to vote in higher numbers than previous elections, and they are expected to hold some 17 seats. Netanyahu’s claim will be that they should not be part of any governing coalition.

Unfortunately for Netanyahu, the two parties who represent the Arab Palestinians of Israel have made it clear that they will do everything to topple Bibi’s far right coalition, and now they can deliver this promise to the voters.

Netanyahu, by aligning himself with the far right and by placing Itamar Ben-Gvir in charge of the police, has mobilised the Arab voters, who have been suffering from a spike of racism since he established this anti-Arab alliance.
If Netanyahu was a leader in a different country, you might expect him to admit his defeat and resign from leading his party, which has been shattered.
But not Netanyahu, who is facing a trial on three corruption cases and is clinging to power.
Netanyahu will now be calling for unity, he will say that there is a draw and that the Jewish parties have to unite against the Arabs.

The question will be: Are there cracks in the anti-Netanyahu camp. It seems that all the six leaders of the anti-Netanyahu camp — Jews and Arabs alike — are determined to do anything they can to oust Netanyahu and his allies. This of course would mean violating the election promises given by some members of the camp that said they would not lean on the Arab vote. Netanyahu cannot pretend to be too surprised if that happens. After all, throughout his campaign he was saying that this is exactly what Eisenkot would do if he had the upper hand.
Voters share their opinions at Machane Yehuda markets in Jerusalem
Ahead of election day, ABC reporters went to the Machane Yehuda market in Jersualem to ask voters what they thought.
Here's what some of them said.

"I think there's no person in this country who can lead us except for Bibi. Listen, he knows what he's doing, he has courage, he has good relations with America, with Trump. I don't think there is anyone else who can do what he wants with force and to come and attack Iran and eliminate Khamenei and Hezbollah and to fight everyone."

"I vote for Shas Deri [ultra-Orthodox, right-wing religious political party] because this is the party of Rav Ovadia. We are Haredi people. We have always voted for Shas. It is important for us to have a Jewish identity in the country, Jewish education for every child. And usually Shas goes with Bibi. This is our way. We are right wing, full right wing."

"My name is Soheir and I'm from the village of Sajur, a Druze village in the north of the land of Israel. Tomorrow I'm voting for [Itamar] Ben-Gvir. I'm sure he is a strong man and he will lead all our country to very unique paths. And that's it. Ben-Gvir is strong. Ben-Gvir is strong."
Foreign minister says 'celebrations on the left are premature'
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar who merged his party with Likud before the election has warned people against getting ahead of themselves.

"The celebrations on the left are premature," he wrote on X."The smugness of the biased commentators — ridiculous. One thing seems quite clear: Likud is the largest party in Israel. It's always good to learn something from the past."
"The celebrations on the left are premature," he wrote on X.
"The smugness of the biased commentators — ridiculous. One thing seems quite clear: Likud is the largest party in Israel. It's always good to learn something from the past."
Underneath, he posted a video from the Likud party's first win in 1977.
No clear path to power, according to exit polls
Israel's election appears deadlocked, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor rival Gadi Eisenkot showing a clear path to power, exit polls show.
The stalemate could work in Netanyahu's favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.

The final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers. No single party has ever won 61 seats outright in the 120-seat Knesset, making coalitions the norm.
The vote drew a record turnout as Israelis passed wartime judgment on Netanyahu in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

Current opposition head Yair Lapid said in a statement: "Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home."

The major networks showed the Eisenkot-led bloc winning between 52 and 53 seats and the Netanyahu-led bloc winning about 50 seats. The remaining 17 to 18 seats were allocated to unaligned Arab parties in the exit polls.
Some Israeli media outlets, including pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, projected a far stronger showing for Netanyahu and his parties, saying they would collectively win 60 seats.
Reuters
How could the election impact Israel's relationship with the United States?

For Israelis, their nation's relationship with the United States is its standout most important relationship. The US's financial support for Israel, along with the close military and intelligence relationship, is seen by Israelis as crucial to their survival.
That relationship is unlikely to change according to whoever is elected in Israel. Both major contenders — Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot — will want it to continue.

The problem for Israel, however, is at the American end. While Donald Trump belatedly endorsed Netanyahu, his relationship with the Israeli PM has been rocky (remember the "f***ing crazy" phone call over Lebanon, as reported by Axios in June?). And from that relationship, it is clear that there are concerns in Washington about Israel's direction.

US Vice-President JD Vance has also revealed a growing crack in the friendship. In June he was asked by media about reports in Israel that Israeli politicians were criticising his attempts to find an end to the Iran war. He said: "If I was in the cabinet of the Israeli government, I might not be attacking the only powerful ally that I have anywhere left in the entire world."

As professional politicians, both Trump and Vance would be conscious of the changing mood in the American public. In April 2026 Pew Research found 60 per cent of American adults had an unfavourable view of Israel. And a Gallup poll in early 2026 found that more Americans sympathised with Palestinians than they did Israelis — 41 per cent to 36 per cent.

Ten years ago the idea that more Americans would sympathise with Palestinians than Israelis would have been unthinkable. The change is largely due to the devastation of Gaza. While most Americans supported Israel's right to respond to Hamas's attacks on October 7, the reduction of Gaza, a home to 2.1 million Palestinians, to "rubble" — a word used by Trump — has changed the reality.
So whatever the outcome of the Israeli election, Israel has a much deeper problem: how it is increasingly being seen by Americans.
What are the key issues driving voters?

Israel is a country which seems to be in a perpetual state of war. Its backers will say it's protecting itself. Its critics will say it brings it on itself by having an aggressive posture in the region.
Regardless of which view people have, national security — or who can keep Israel safe — is a central theme in this election.
Netanyahu’s reputation as "Mr Security" took a battering on October 7, 2023, as Hamas launched its surprise raids and carried out the deadliest attack on Israel since its establishment in 1948.
Since then, wars with Hezbollah in Lebanon and against the Iranian regime in Tehran have put Israel in a precarious position – regardless of its military might.
None of the challengers to Netanyahu are promising wholesale change on management of those multiple wars.
But some of the issues that have erupted because of the conflicts are dominating election debates.

There are calls for a totally independent inquiry into the failures which allowed the October 7 attacks to occur — something Netanyahu has repeatedly rejected. His rivals, including Gadi Eisenkot, are promising such a probe.

The multiple wars have also put the issue of resourcing for the military on the agenda. Every Israeli is meant to complete their compulsory military service when they turn 18, and many continue to perform reserve duty afterwards. The ultra-Orthodox Jewish community was exempt from that until the Supreme Court tore up the policy in 2024.
Critics have accused Netanyahu, whose coalition includes ultra-Orthodox parties that refused to yield on demands to restore the exemptions, of failing to fix the issue.

Issues like the cost of living are also present in the campaign, given Israel is one of the most expensive countries in the OECD. Fuel (95 unleaded) recently had to be capped at 7.77 shekels a litre, which is roughly $3.60.
But it takes a back seat to the greater security and societal problems the country is facing.
The Israelis who flew home to vote
Tens of thousands of Israeli citizens abroad, including estimates of hundreds from Australia, have travelled to Israel to vote in the country's most consequential election in decades.

Political activists mobilised around the world to bring Israeli citizens overseas to the country to vote, given ballots can only be cast in person on election day, with exceptions for serving soldiers and diplomats.

The AID Coalition, a US-based non-profit which describes itself as non-partisan,estimates that as many as 67,000 voters are returning to Israel, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its Fly&Vote initiative.
It says about half are flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
Among those who have travelled to Israel is Anat Dror, who has been living in Melbourne for almost five years and recently became an Australian citizen.
She said she had flown to Israel to vote against Benjamin Netanyahu:
"The sentiment for us is that right now, voting is absolutely essential. It's something that absolutely comes from the heart and no-one would be able to talk me out of it," she told the ABC.

"I'm coming here at the very expensive cost of missing out on work days and paying for a very expensive ticket and missing my kids at home … All of these are not deterring any of us from coming here to vote.
"This is our motherland and our motherland needs us right now."
Supporters of various parties celebrate in streets as polls close
Netanyahu opponent warns against scare tactics

Walking into the polling station in Herzliya, you are met with blaring music. Dozens of journalists and voters have gathered to see the man many are hoping will be the next prime minister and unseat Netanyahu.
Gadi Eisenkot is swarmed by crowds as he climbs the stairs of a local school to cast his vote.

After casting his vote, the leader of Yashar — a word meaning straight — addresses the press and the crowd of supporters who have gathered in a school. Chants of "our next prime minister" are heard as the crowd is hushed for the former military chief to speak.

“I call on all Israeli citizens to go vote, not to be deterred by the heat and the disturbances, to stay committed to the mission, to replace the worst government since the state was founded, tonight.”
The leader of the centrist Yashar party criticised Netanyahu’s attempt to derail the election and what he said were the prime minister’s scare tactics.
For Eisenkot, this was "the most critical day, perhaps since the founding of the state".

Voters at the polling station were casting their ballots for a variety of candidates. We spoke to some who said it was imperative that the country change. For one voter, it was the last chance for democracy.
"It's catastrophe. It’s four years of catastrophe," one voter named Mirijam said.
"The people of Israel are smart people but the people upstairs are terrible," she said.
📹: Benjamin Netanyahu supporters in the Likud HQ
What do these polls actually mean?
Dear readers, you may well be bamboozled by the various exit polls coming from the Israeli media now that voting in the Israeli election has finished.
What does it all mean?
Well, it's safe to say that Yashar will not be thrilled to be running second to Likud in terms of being the largest party in the Knesset.
All of the public polling to this point had suggested it would be in the box seat.
Likud will be crowing about this, and Benjamin Netanyahu will chalk it up as a win for his campaign and a win for the right wing of Israeli politics.

But even while Yashar has run second, there's still hope for the anti-Netanyahu bloc, with strong figures coming from the Together joint list of former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid and the Democrats.

And the far-right parties that have propped up the Netanyahu coalition in this last term, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich (settlers who have been sanctioned by countries including Australia) will only secure six seats each.
That undermines the Netanyahu bid for forming a coalition.
The other standout here is a strong showing for the Arab parties, often referred to as the Palestinian parties.

High voter turnout among the Arab-Palestinian population, which is 20 per cent of Israel's community, seem to have lifted their standing — the Joint List into double digits, the United Arab List not far behind.
Netanyahu has railed against them in the campaign, trying to de-legitimise them in the eyes of voters.
As much as Israeli politics can throw up some strange bedfellows, it's safe to say the Joint List and United Arab List would be in the sights of the anti-Netanyahu bloc to get them over the line.
How has October 7 shaped the public's perceptions of Netanyahu and his government?
Hamas's deadly attacks on October 7, 2023, continue to cast a long shadow over Israel, Gaza and the broader Middle East region.
What allowed the attacks to happen, as well as how Benjamin Netanyahu handled them, is expected to play a huge role in how Israelis vote this election.

Netanyahu has spent his entire political career carefully cultivating an image of being the security hard man — the man the nation can trust to not only identify and call out threats, but to keep Israelis safe from them.
The October 7 attacks put that image through the shredder. And he's arguably spent the past three years being even more aggressive to try to restore it.

Netanyahu regularly pushes an idea labelled by the Israeli media as "the betrayal theory" or "the treason theory" — a claim he was deliberately kept in the dark by senior defence and intelligence officials about the threat massing at the Gaza border. He has gone as far as to say he wasn't woken up early enough on October 7 to deal with the response.
His political rivals have seized on this defensiveness in their election campaigning, promising that shirking responsibility will become a thing of the past.

Opponents have also pointed to the most extreme voices in the Netanyahu coalition — people like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich (both long-time settlers who have been sanctioned by governments around the world, including Australia, for their policies and rhetoric against Palestinians) — as evidence of how the prime minister has allowed his own desire to hold on to power dictate his government's decision making , arguing extremists are taking Israel down a dangerous path.
An update from Yashar HQ
Yashar anthems are blasting, across all genres from pop to folk, to house to hip hop, as journalists fill the room and anticipation builds for the camp that has vowed to bring change.
It's clear there is a long night ahead.
As polls came in, the music picked up, flags were raised and cheers erupted.
Even though there is no clear winner yet, Eizenkot’s team here told ABC news they are confident this means victory, and that they are on the right track.

Exit polls show Netanyahu's Likud party on track to be largest in Knesset
Polls have closed in the Israeli election, with exit polls from the nation’s media outlets showing Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is likely to be the largest party in the next Knesset.
But it is still unclear whether he will be able to form a coalition government, with the anti-Netanyahu parties recording a significant share of the vote.
Israel’s public broadcaster, KAN, says Likud is on track to secure 25 seats, while challenger Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar will secure 21 seats.
Commercial network Channel 13 is reporting Likud will also receive 25 seats, while Yashar will get 23.
Taking into account the likely coalition partners, the anti-Netanyahu bloc, which includes Yashar, Together, and the Democrats, are still ahead by a handful of seats.
The far-right parties which had propped up the Netanyahu government in the last term of government, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are likely to secure only six seats each.
Could the Arab-Israeli parties end up holding the balance of power?
There were a lot of unknowns in this campaign, and one was them was how many Israelis would cast a vote. Voting is not compulsory in Israel, but records have been broken tonight.
One group which could have a profound impact on the result is the Palestinian citizens of Israel, often referred to as Arab-Israelis.

Traditionally, they have a much lower turnout than the general population. This is a group which feels not only marginalised from the rest of the country but actively discriminated against in terms of policies and resources. Palestinian communities face high crime and poverty rates, among other issues.
But, they make up 20 per cent of the Israeli population.
If these voters showed up and voted, many would likely back the "Arab-Israeli" parties, the United Arab List and the Joint List.
That could put those two blocs in a position of considerable influence in the days and weeks after election day.
On Friday, Channels 11, 12, 13 and newspaper Maariv all put the Joint List at securing nine seats. The same outlets put the United Arab List at securing between five and seven seats.
That puts the two groups in a position where the larger parties, particularly Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, could approach them for support in any coalition agreement.

During the campaign, Netanyahu railed against the idea of cooperation with the Palestinian-dominated parties. Opposition leaders including Eisenkot have also distanced themselves from talk of cooperation with the Joint List or the United Arab List.
But in the mad scramble for power, unlikely bedfellows could quickly emerge, even as Israel remains deeply divided.

Voter turnout breaks records across Israel
Israelis have streamed to the polls in record numbers.
The Central Elections Committee reports voter turnout at 74.3 per cent.
Forecasters were hesitant to guess what impact the strong turnout might have on the result.

A surge in votes from Israelis of Palestinian heritage could limit gains for Mr Netanyahu's right-wing coalition and make it more likely that any government formed to oust him would require Arab parties' support, a contentious prospect among Jewish party leaders.
Ahmed Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said record turnout from Israel's Arab minority would "pave the way for an alternative government and change the grave reality".
Reuters

The polls have now closed
It is now 10pm in Israel and the polls have closed.
Voters have turned out in record numbers and now we wait to see who will lead Israel.
That result won't be immediately apparent, but stick with us as we bring you the latest.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot cast their votes
Voters 'know what they want' according to former Knesset member
At the polling station in Rehavia, we picked out of the crowd a familiar face in Israeli politics.
Mossi Raz has been a member of the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, having represented the former left-wing Meretz party from 2000 to 2003, 2017 to 2019, and 2021 to 2022.
This time, he's running for The Democrats, which is the party formed out of the merger of Meretz and the former Labor party.
Anyway, Mossi was fairly clear eyed about how he believed voters would be behave at the ballot box.
"There is a feeling of people, unlike previous elections campaigns, know what they want,” he said.
The Democrats are one of the parties which commentators argue will likely join with other anti-Netanyahu parties, such as Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, to form a coalition.
I asked Mossi whether he was worried about polling showing support from the right wing of Israeli voters still propping up the prime minister's Likud party and others in his current government.

“The groups who support Netanyahu in the society grew increased in this last four years," he said.“There are more religious people, more settlers, more ultra-orthodox, and many liberals who left the country.“The opposition was very successful in turning people who were supporters of Netanyahu last time to vote for the opposition.
“The groups who support Netanyahu in the society grew increased in this last four years," he said.
“There are more religious people, more settlers, more ultra-orthodox, and many liberals who left the country.
“The opposition was very successful in turning people who were supporters of Netanyahu last time to vote for the opposition.
Raz said after polling day, there would be a test for the anti-Netanyahu camp.

“The only question is if it is enough and if the heads of the opposition, I hope the next prime minister, will be honest enough to cooperate with the two Arab Palestinian lists because without them [a change of government] will not happen.”
What does the election look like in Israel's suburbs
Having covered Australian politics for a few years before moving to Jerusalem, I can tell you the election looks and feels somewhat familiar when voters are arriving at polling stations.
It was just a bit messier because there are so many more parties running.

Just like in Australia, there are party volunteers lining up outside the entrances armed with flyers trying to win over voters at the last minute. Although in Rehavia, a more affluent Jerusalem suburb, they weren't as aggressive as they may have been in other parts of the country.
There were also no democracy sausages on offer.
A lot of the campaign material focuses on white slips of paper with Hebrew letters on them. This reflects how Israeli voters actually cast their ballot.
Rather than marking a piece of paper, each voter picks a ballot with the lettering representing their desired party and puts it in an envelope.

Parties pick their lettering based on part of their messaging. Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar has a ballot paper saying the Hebrew word for "way" or "street", saying a vote for it is a vote to put Israel on the right path.
Others are more obscure.
I did see some racist campaign material from one of the far-right Haredi parties, called Noam, littered on the ground.
It showed a number of Muslim women and a slogan along the lines of: "Are these the people you want to teach your children?"
Noam is not expected to secure enough votes to secure even a single seat in the Knesset.
And some of the other right-wing party volunteers were having a crack at their team, saying they were pinching votes from the parties which do have a chance of getting in.

Who is Gadi Eisenkot, the main opponent facing Netanyahu?

There are a handful of parties all trying to chip away at Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party. But few seem to have garnered as much support, at least in terms of public polling, as the brand new Yashar party led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants and a former chief of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) — a position he held under Mr Netanyahu from 2015 to 2019.
After retiring from the military he entered politics, joining Benny Gantz's Blue and White party.
It's interesting to note here that Mr Gantz, a one-time high flyer in the Israeli political system, pulled out of this election a week out from polling day because his numbers were so poor.

After the deadly October 7 attacks by Hamas in October 2023, Eisenkot joined the emergency war cabinet — an attempt by Mr Netanyahu to bring together politicians from outside his ruling coalition to show unity of purpose after the terrorist attacks.
But Eisenkot, and Gantz, quit a few months later. And this is where the cracks in the relationship between Eisenkot and Netanyahu really started to emerge.
He accused the government of being beholden to extreme right-wing voices, making decisions about the war which were more about annihilation of an enemy rather than the safety of Israeli hostages.
In mid-2025, he quit the Knesset altogether. A few months later, he established Yashar — which translates to "straight" or "honest".

Netanyahu has spent a lot of time trying to paint Eisenkot as an inept leader and weak on security. He says the former general's grasp on English is weak, calling that a problem for a country like Israel on the world stage. The prime minister also accuses him of being prepared to roll over to Israel's enemies.

But Netanyahu's criticism overlooks one of the key markers in Eisenkot's military career: He was the man who developed the so-called Dahiyeh Doctrine, named after the Hezbollah stronghold suburbs in southern Beirut. It calls for the disproportionate use of force against an enemy, to effectively bomb them into submission.
'No doubt' it's time for Netanyahu to go
Back in Rehavia, a few more voters shared their views on the election with us.
Menachem Lorberbaum said his vote was "private" when asked who he backed at the ballot box.
But he said there was "no doubt" it was time for a change of leadership.

"You don't have to vote for [Gadi] Eisenkot or for anybody, you know, on that side to see that, to speak to people on the street and they'll tell you that people have to know when it's time to go home," he said.
Menachem added that Israel was "undergoing a very deep realignment" of values and attitudes.
"The shifts and the deep divides are elsewhere from where they were 30 years ago, and I think you see this quite dramatically," he said.

Israel is in a different place today ... no democracy is perfect, no polity is perfect, but I think that this is one of the most dramatic tests of the ability of the self-corrective principles within a republic, a democratic republic, to renew itself.”
That division Menachem was speaking about was perhaps evident on some of the Likud party flyers being handed out to voters as they arrived at the primary school.
For weeks, Mr Netanyahu has painted his political opponents as being supporters of the Palestinian cause, as he tried to whip up support and fear about the issue.

His flyers read "Right or Palestine", which in Hebrew rhymes, and featured photos of the anti-Netanyahu party leaders such as Gadi Eisenkot, Yair Golan, Avigdor Liberman and the leaders of the two Arab-Palestinian groups running at the election, Yousef Jabareen and Mansour Abbas.
Netanyahu supporter Etti Brand was clutching one as she arrived to vote.
"He is the only one," she said of the prime minister when asked who she was voting for."Yair Golan and Eisenkot are going to bring us to Palestine."
"He is the only one," she said of the prime minister when asked who she was voting for.
"Yair Golan and Eisenkot are going to bring us to Palestine."
Voters divided on whether it's time for Netanyahu to 'go home'
We spent a bit of time talking to voters at a primary school in the Jerusalem suburb of Rehavia earlier in the day.
It's just around the corner from Benjamin Netanyahu's personal residence in the city, and a short drive from the prime minister's official Jerusalem home.
It was also where Israeli president Isaac Herzog cast his ballot.
Something we've heard a lot in recent weeks from critics of Mr Netanyahu is that it's "time for him to go home".
And some of the residents we spoke to certainly agreed with that sentiment.
Meira Partem didn't say which party she specifically backed, but said she had voted for a "new dawn" — a government without Mr Netanyahu at the helm.

"First of all, it's not democratic, it's the same prime minister for so many years."The second thing, after this terrible semi-Holocaust that happened here in my Jewish sovereign state, anyone should have stepped down and apologised."And the gall not to do that is very, very disturbing.”
"First of all, it's not democratic, it's the same prime minister for so many years.
"The second thing, after this terrible semi-Holocaust that happened here in my Jewish sovereign state, anyone should have stepped down and apologised.
"And the gall not to do that is very, very disturbing.”
She's talking there about accountability for the defence and security failures which allowed the October 7 attacks to occur in 2023, when about 1,200 Israelis were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
Meira described the prime minister as an "opportunist" who would work with any partner as long as it meant holding on to power.
"If a prime minister tries to have everybody loyal to him, and not to the country, not to the law, that's destructive to the country," she said.
Mr Netanyahu did have support in Rehavia.
"I'm voting Bibi, obviously, because he's our wartime leader and we're still mid-war," voter Yosef Abraham told us.
"I think anybody who wants the government to switch is actually anti-Israel, he wants us to get weaker, because midwar, you don't change leadership.
"I think we need other leadership in different times, but right now we have to continue to support Bibi."
Mr Abraham had very strong views about Palestinian and Arab citizens of Israel, insisting they needed to assimilate or leave.
"Each Arab can place the flag of Israel in their schools, in their houses, and then they remain citizens," he said."If they refuse, they are our enemy from within, and we need to cleanse them out."
"Each Arab can place the flag of Israel in their schools, in their houses, and then they remain citizens," he said.
"If they refuse, they are our enemy from within, and we need to cleanse them out."
20 per cent of Israel's population are of Palestinian or Arab descent, and they typically have a much lower turnout at elections due to decades of marginalisation.

Inside Netanyahu's HQ
It's still early, and polls haven't closed.
No members of the public are filling the hall at the moment.
There are bundles of Likud party placards sitting in plastic wrapping on the side of the room, for when those supporters do materialise.
We're in a large hall in central Jerusalem, along with hundreds of journalists from around the world.
Hopefully the internet holds out.
Welcome to today's live coverage
Good morning.
While you were sleeping, Israeli citizens voted for their next prime minister.
The polls are set to close in the next hour, but due to the country's parliamentary system, the winner won't be immediately obvious.
In Israel, the leader who can assemble a governing coalition with a majority of 61 or more Knesset seats takes office and this can take several weeks of political negotiations.
The incumbent, Benjamin Netanyahu, has polled poorly leading into the election despite an endorsement from great ally Donald Trump.
After three years of Israel's war with Gaza and most recently the war it launched with the US against Iran in February, the world has its eyes on the outcome of the election.
To make sense of the complex political system and what it means internationally and on Australian shores, Middle East correspondents and academics will join us on the blog this morning.
Have a question? Log in to comment below.
